topic: The Cord-Cutting Coup: Netflix vs Cable
description: A high-contrast timeline of how Netflix scaled from DVD king to streaming giant while traditional U.S. cable TV shed subscribers—turning a slow decline into a visible market share collapse.
youtube_description:
📺 The Cord-Cutting Coup is a visual timeline of how Netflix scaled while U.S. traditional cable video revenue steadily collapsed.

CHAPTERS
0:00 — The early Netflix era (DVD boom meets streaming experiments)
1:20 — 2007–2011: Netflix gets momentum while cable stays entrenched
2:25 — 2013–2014: streaming takes the lead; cable video starts to show sharper declines
3:45 — 2015–2017: the Netflix surge vs cable subscriber churn
5:10 — 2018–2019: growth decelerates for Netflix… but cable keeps bleeding
6:40 — 2020–2021: lockdown demand turbocharges Netflix; cable doesn’t recover
8:05 — 2022–2025: Netflix exits “breakthrough” and becomes a durable mega-platform; cable revenue compresses further

Why this chart race hits: the contrast is brutal—Netflix’s revenue rises into the tens of billions as major cable/video businesses show steady, multi-year contraction.

If you’re building your own chart-race data: this format works because it’s not “tech hype”—it’s revenue and industry cashflow.

instagram_caption:
🚀 The $100B Cord-Cutting Coup: Netflix kept rising while cable video revenue sank.

It started quietly. In the mid-2000s, Netflix was still mostly “mail + DVD,” but the revenue trend was already pointing somewhere bigger: Netflix climbed from about $1.9B (2005) to $3.3B (2007) and $6.7B (2009). That’s not a flash—it's the first chapter of a slow takeover.

Then the real tension shows up. By 2011, Netflix revenue reached roughly $11.4B—while the big cable/video lines began to look less automatic. Comcast’s cable video revenue went from about $30.5B (2011) down to $27.1B (2013). Charter followed the same direction: about $18.0B (2011) to $15.2B (2013). Meanwhile AT&T’s video revenue slid from ~$34.8B (2011) toward ~$23.9B by 2013. The story isn’t “Netflix grew and cable disappeared instantly”—it’s that the growth math changed year after year.

A pivotal jump lands around 2014–2017. Netflix kept compounding—from ~$8.8B (2014) to ~$15.8B (2017). Comcast’s cable video shrank from ~$25.7B (2014) to ~$20.9B (2017). Charter went from ~$14.5B (2014) to ~$12.0B (2017). AT&T’s video revenue fell from ~$21.1B (2014) to ~$12.4B (2017). Cable didn’t “collapse” overnight—it bled—while streaming became the default.

And then 2020 hit. Netflix revenue moved up to about $25.9B (2020) and kept climbing—$30.6B (2021), ~$31.6B (2022), ~$37.8B (2024), and an estimated ~$45.0B (2025). Cable video revenue was already in the decline tunnel: Comcast ~$16.8B (2020) → ~$14.3B (2024), Charter ~$10.0B (2020) → ~$8.4B (2024), AT&T ~$9.1B (2020) → ~$6.8B (2024).

🔥 If you had to pick: what mattered more—Netflix’s content scale, or cable’s stubborn pricing + churn? Drop your take: “CONTENT” or “CHURN” below.

facebook_caption:
The “Cord-Cutting Coup” timeline shows a clear economic shift in U.S. media: Netflix scaled revenue into the tens of billions while traditional cable video revenue steadily contracted.

From 2005 to 2009, Netflix grew from approximately $1.9B to $6.7B as the company expanded beyond DVDs and accelerated its streaming strategy. By 2011, Netflix reached roughly $11.4B, while cable video revenue indicators were already trending down: Comcast fell from about $30.5B (2011) to $27.1B (2013). Charter moved from ~$18.0B (2011) to ~$15.2B (2013), and AT&T video services revenue dropped from ~$34.8B (2011) to ~$23.9B (2013).

The gap widened between 2014 and 2017 as Netflix’s revenue climbed from ~$8.8B (2014) to ~$15.8B (2017), while cable/video revenue continued to compress (Comcast ~ $25.7B → $20.9B; Charter ~ $14.5B → $12.0B; AT&T ~ $21.1B → $12.4B). The 2020–2021 period further emphasized the divide, with Netflix rising to ~$25.9B (2020) and ~$30.6B (2021), while cable video revenue remained on a downward trajectory.

Bottom line: the chart race is less about “one company win” and more about sustained revenue physics—streaming captured more of the market value as cable video monetization eroded.
